newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU citizens evenly divided on Euro.
newsitem.headline: EU citizens evenly divided on Euro.

text.p: European Union leaders might just as well have saved themselves the trouble of taking hours to fudge a deal on the future of the Euro at their summit in Amsterdam on Monday. Most people are against it or don't care.

A survey published in Brussels on Tuesday by French bank Sofinco showed that 43 percent of people surveyed thought the introduction of the Euro, the EU's much-debated single currency, would be more inconvenient than beneficial.
Another 25 percent either didn't know or couldn't say, while 32 percent were in favour.
The telephone survey of a total of just over 6,000 people over the age of 15 years in France, Germany, Britain, Spain, Italy, Belgium and the Netherlands was conducted between May 16 and 28.
Most against were the Germans with a figure of 57 percent, followed by French and Britons on 48 percent and the Dutch on 41 percent.

Most in favour were Italians, whose bid to be in the vanguard of nations joining the Euro in January 1999 has been a highly contentious issue among the EU's monetary purists, with a figure of 40 percent.
A total of 45 percent of Spaniards simply didn't know either way, while Belgians were fairly evenly divided between the three categories.
On a separate but more immediately relevant issue, the citizens of the seven nations split into two camps on their views of the general economic climate.
Britons and Dutch were strongly optimistic about their situation, with Spaniards running a close third.
In total 79 percent of the Dutch were either optimistic or strongly optimistic, with 73 percent of Britons and 57 percent of Spaniards feeling the same way.
By contrast 72 percent of Germans were either pessimistic or strongly pessimistis, with 69 percent of Belgians, 66 percent of Italians and 64 percent of French sharing that view.

The average among the seven nations -- whose citizens between them account for 80 percent of consumption in the 15-nation EU, was 54 percent pessimistic and 43 percent optimistic. Three percent didn't know.
